papers.title: Bayesian Nonparametric Survival Regression with Time-Varying Covariates and Random Effects
papers.abstract: In longitudinal survival studies, biomarkers and treatments change across visits, their associations with event risk may be nonlinear and change over time, and subjects with identical measurements may differ in risk. Existing tree-ensemble survival models address these features separately: discrete-time formulations accommodate covariate updates without subject-specific random effects, and hazard-based ensembles with frailty take covariates as fixed at baseline. We propose Time-Varying Survival Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (TVSurvBART), a continuous-time hazard model combining a flexible baseline, a log-linear tree ensemble, and subject-specific random intercepts and slopes; covariates enter as predictable step processes, and interval-start time among the tree inputs lets effects change across visits. Integrated exposure offsets absorb the within-interval variation of the baseline and random slopes, so the tree leaves retain conjugate updates. Re-centering moves along likelihood-invariant directions and alternating centered and non-centered covariance updates address the resulting posterior dependence. In two simulation families, TVSurvBART's landmark predictions from held-out subjects' histories up to the landmark time have higher time-dependent AUC than the Cox, frailty Cox, and forest benchmarks in every setting and lower Brier scores in all but one comparison, although population-summary gains are not uniform. In the CARRA juvenile idiopathic arthritis registry, discrimination for recorded flares is similar to Cox regression, while a secondary interval-probability score favors TVSurvBART.

papers.title: Single-fit inference for the realized prediction error of a logistic model with many predictors
papers.abstract: When independent validation data are unavailable, evaluating a fitted logistic model on new patients requires estimating prediction error and uncertainty. Evaluating the fit on training data is often optimistic. Bootstrap validation is widely used to correct this bias, but with many predictors, it can retain bias and yield unreliable confidence intervals. In this article, we study these limitations and develop single-fit estimation and inference without resampling. When the number of Gaussian predictors grows proportionally with sample size, we analyze unpenalized logistic models. We prove that standard bootstrap correction can have nonzero limiting bias even as the resample count grows and location-shifted intervals can have zero limiting coverage. Instead, we adjust the fitted scores to consistently estimate realized Brier and log losses. We account for common fitting and adjustment error to construct valid marginal intervals and joint regions. We also establish these single-fit estimation and inference guarantees for certain non-Gaussian designs in proportional dimensions. Under moderate dimension growth and possible misspecification with general predictors, we extend single-fit inference to ridge regularization and construct asymptotically valid confidence intervals for realized log loss. Simulations and analyses of hospital and diabetes datasets support our theory and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

papers.title: Faithful Generative Modeling for Censored Time-to-Event Data: From Distributional Fidelity to Statistical Inference
papers.abstract: Synthetic data has emerged as a powerful tool for data sharing, clinical trial simulation, and digital twin development, with growing applications in biomedical research and drug development. However, limited attention has been devoted to synthetic time-to-event data, which are central to clinical trials and survival analysis. In particular, theoretical guarantees for the distributional fidelity of synthetic survival data remain largely unexplored. More importantly, even when a generator achieves distributional fidelity, it remains unclear whether the downstream statistical analysis is reliable. To address these gaps, we propose a general two-stage generative framework for survival data (TSGSurv) that jointly generates observed times and covariates conditional on event status, and establish its distributional convergence rate. Focusing on the widely used Cox proportional hazards model, we establish conditions under which generator fidelity guarantees consistency of model coefficient estimates. We further characterize the limitations of naive inference based on synthetic data, and develop a variance correction and a distribution calibration procedure to recover valid inference of original data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed generative and inferential framework with extensive simulations and two real data applications.

papers.title: Adaptive Tests of Pricing Restrictions with Observed and Latent Factors
papers.abstract: This paper develops a high-dimensional test for asset pricing models with observed and latent factors. The null hypothesis allows the intercepts from an observed-factor regression to be nonzero, provided that they lie in the latent factor loading space. We estimate the pricing errors in three steps: regress returns on the observed factors, extract latent factors from the lagged covariance structure of the regression residuals, and regress returns on both observed and estimated latent factors. The intercept from the final regression serves as the estimated pricing error. We construct Sum and Max tests based on the estimated pricing errors to detect diffuse and concentrated alternatives, respectively, and combine them using a Cauchy procedure. Under suitable regularity conditions, we establish the joint null distribution of the component statistics, their asymptotic independence, and their power against alternative hypotheses. We also propose a residual bootstrap and establish its first-order validity. Simulation studies examine the finite-sample performance of the tests under different pricing-error patterns and factor-number choices. An application to S\&P 500 stocks illustrates the use of the proposed framework in evaluating an observed-factor pricing model after latent-factor adjustment.

papers.title: A Unified Unfolding and Slide-Vector Model for Asymmetric Dissimilarities via Clustered Lasso
papers.abstract: Asymmetric multidimensional scaling (AMDS) methods represent asymmetric dissimilarity data in a low-dimensional space. Existing approaches include the highly flexible unfolding model and the parsimonious slide-vector model. However, a highly flexible model is not necessarily optimal for adequately representing asymmetric relationships, and a model with an intermediate level of complexity may be more effective. In this study, we propose a new AMDS model that integrates the unfolding and slide-vector models by incorporating a clustered Lasso penalty. By fusing similar slide vectors, the proposed method can represent intermediate model structures and adjust model complexity according to the observed data. In numerical simulations, we compared the proposed method with existing methods by varying the number of groups, the number of objects, and the number of dimensions. The results demonstrated that the proposed method achieved high estimation accuracy across various asymmetric structures. Furthermore, in an application to cola brand-switching data, the proposed method achieved the highest accuracy in reproducing asymmetric relationships among the three methods compared and yielded a lower stress value than the slide-vector model. These findings suggest that adaptively adjusting model complexity may be effective for representing asymmetric relationships more accurately.

papers.title: Matrix elliptical sliced inverse regression: structured dimension reduction for heavy-tailed data
papers.abstract: Sliced inverse regression is widely used for sufficient dimension reduction, but existing matrix extensions that rely on covariance-based statistics can be unstable under heavy-tailed distributions. We propose matrix elliptical sliced inverse regression (MESIR) for estimating response-relevant row and column reduction subspaces under matrix elliptical distributions. We establish a mode-wise linearity relation linking the inverse regression curve to these subspaces through the corresponding scatter matrices. MESIR combines inverse-regression Kendall's tau matrices with eigenvalue-calibrated marginal Kendall's tau matrices. The calibration recovers the row and column scatter matrices needed to identify the reduction subspaces. Theoretically, we derive convergence rates for the calibrated marginal and inverse-regression estimators and establish subspace consistency under weak moment conditions, allowing the matrix dimensions and number of slices to diverge with the sample size. We further develop a consistent eigenvalue-ratio procedure for structural dimension selection and extend the method and theory to higher-order tensor predictors. Thorough simulation studies are conducted to show competitive performance under light tails and increasingly pronounced gains as the tails become heavier. Applications to COVID-19 CT images and radar target recognition demonstrate favorable empirical performance.

papers.title: On the trajectories of the ID algorithm
papers.abstract: The ID algorithm decides whether an interventional distribution can be computed from observational data and, when it can, returns a formula in which products, ratios and summations of conditional probabilities are nested inside one another. We study these formulas by following the trajectories of the calls of the algorithm, each of which ends with a tail (an alternation of lines 7 and 2) and an exit, and we derive two main results. First, line~4 and the exit lines fix the single outer summation of the output, while the tail forms everything inside it, both the inner summations and the ratios. Second, a ratio keeps a summation in its denominator only when a repetition of the tail is entangled, and a test of ancestry in the original graph decides, before any formula is computed, whether a topological order can be chosen so as to avoid it. We also derive a bound on the nesting depth of the output, and show a simple ``dimensional'' count that every output has to satisfy. Together, these results constrain the form of an ID output and guide its implementation and simplification.

papers.title: General Methodology for Asymptotically Balanced Multiple Tests
papers.abstract: In statistical applications, often more than one hypothesis is of interest and, thus, multiple testing problems occur naturally. To control the family-wise error rate, popular adjustment methods, like the Bonferroni and Holm correction, have been developed. However, these methods do not use the dependence structure of the test statistics. Consequently, they are conservative in most settings. To increase the power of the tests, the joint dependence structure of the test statistics can be incorporated for the construction of critical values, for example, by using resampling schemes as bootstrap procedures to approximate the joint distribution. This has already been applied in several contexts. In this work, we develop a very flexible and general theoretical foundation, which can be used to construct asymptotically balanced multiple tests that control the family-wise error rate in the strong sense. Additionally, we prove in the general setting that consistent resampling schemes satisfy the needed conditions.

papers.title: Fully Bayesian Benchmarking for Small Area Models with Count Data
papers.abstract: Small area estimates of counts are often required to conform exactly to reliable aggregates at a higher geographic level. Often the area-level model is specified on a transformed (nonlinear) scale such as a log scale. Specifying the small area model on the log-scale is common practice for positive responses. A prominent example is the production of the Small Area Income and Poverty Estimates (SAIPE) by the US Census Bureau. When the model is specified in a transformed scale, the benchmarking constraints, which are linear in the area means, become nonlinear in terms of the model parameters. We develop a new class of priors for Bayesian small area models under strict external benchmarking constraints when the small area model is specified in a transformed scale, and the model parameters belong to a Riemannian manifold due to the nonlinear benchmarking constraints. The prior is fully supported on the constrained parameter set, the manifold defined by the benchmarking constraints, and thereby provides a proper constrained posterior that is also supported on the restricted set. This facilitates full Bayesian analysis of the problem without the requirement of post-hoc modification to the posterior to enforce the benchmarking constraints.

papers.title: Elementwise Precision-weighted Compositional Data Analysis by Weighted Alternating Least Squares
papers.abstract: Logratio principal component is a multivariate method commonly used for exploring compositional data sets. This method is mostly used in an unweighted manner, employing the centred logratio transformation of the compositions. The smaller elements of a composition usually have a higher relative error, and can be downweighted using part-wise weighting. In this article we focus on weighting compositional data and propose elementwise precision weighting of compositions. This is particularly convenient for compositions with parts that fluctuate from rare to frequent; e.g. parts acting as traces in some samples, but being abundant in others. We suggest to weight in the logarithmic or logratio scale, with the inverse of the standard deviation of the logratio, the latter being estimated for each part of each composition separately. A weighted least squares algorithm is used for dimension reduction and compositional biplot construction. Several applications of elementwise precision weighting are described, using compositional datasets from genetics, archaeology and microbiomics that illustrate the power and advantages of a fully weighted compositional analysis.

papers.title: Causal Effect Estimation Under Uncertain Statistical Surrogacy
papers.abstract: Surrogate endpoints can improve the efficiency of causal effect estimation, but such gains may depend on structural assumptions. One such assumption is statistical surrogacy, which requires the primary outcome to be conditionally independent of treatment given the surrogate and baseline covariates. We study causal effect estimation with multiple candidate surrogates of uncertain validity under statistical surrogacy, considering settings where the primary outcome is either fully observed or subject to missingness. We characterize the asymptotic efficiency differences between surrogate-assisted and benchmark estimators, examine the bias induced by violations of statistical surrogacy, and identify conditions under which incorporating surrogate information leads to efficiency gains or losses. To address uncertainty in surrogate validity, we propose Surrogate-assisted Adaptive Causal effect EStimation (SACES), a procedure that anchors estimation to a robust benchmark while adaptively selecting among a finite set of surrogate-assisted estimators using an estimated mean squared error criterion. SACES aims to leverage efficiency gains when statistical surrogacy holds while preserving consistency when the assumption is violated. Simulations demonstrate that SACES achieves a favorable bias-variance trade-off across varying degrees of surrogacy violation. We illustrate the proposed methods using data from the ACTG 175 clinical trial to demonstrate how surrogate information can be adaptively incorporated into causal effect estimation.

papers.title: Statistical Inference with Ill-Conditioned Random Weight Neural Network Sieves
papers.abstract: Random weight neural networks (RWNNs) are shallow networks whose hidden-layer parameters are randomly generated and then kept fixed, while only the output coefficients are estimated. Conditional on the sampled parameters, RWNN regression is a linear sieve problem with random approximation space. We show that such random sieves cannot remain uniformly well-conditioned as their dimension grows. For parametrized feature families satisfying polynomial covering and Lipschitz conditions, the eigenvalues of the population covariance matrix are proven to have polynomial upper bounds determined by the covering geometry of the parameter space, leading to a vanishing smallest eigenvalue. We develop approximation, estimation, and inference theory that explicitly treats the ill-conditioning. Under a $\beta$-H\"older source condition, we obtain both faster-than-Monte-Carlo $L^2$ approximation rates and new $L^\infty$ approximation bounds based on stratified sampling. We then derive improved consistency guarantees for ridge-regularized least squares driven by ridge effective dimension, spectral, and leverage-based stability conditions. For inference, we establish asymptotic linearity and Gaussian limits for linear functional directions while allowing the smallest eigenvalue of the population covariance matrix to vanish. Nondegeneracy is directional: we characterize it with a ridge-normalized Rayleigh quotient and extend it to smooth functionals via Riesz representation. Consistency of ridge-adjusted variance estimators is proved, yielding feasible studentized inference. Numerical experiments illustrate the deterioration of random-feature conditioning and the finite-sample behavior of the resulting estimation and inference procedures.

papers.title: Optimal Transport Rank Regression for Robust Multivariate-Response Regression
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose optimal transport rank regression for robust multivariate-response mean regression. The proposed method maps residual distributions to the uniform measure on the unit ball and constructs its loss from the resulting optimal transport ranks. This construction exploits cross-response dependence to improve efficiency while preserving population Fisher consistency and orthogonal invariance. Beyond these population properties, we establish statistical guarantees for the proposed method in both linear and nonparametric regression. For linear models, we establish asymptotic normality, characterise robustness, and develop orthogonally invariant asymptotic inference. We derive a distribution-uniform lower bound on asymptotic efficiency relative to least-squares and demonstrate efficiency gains over coordinatewise methods under several heavy-tailed and contaminated distributions. For nonparametric regression, we establish non-asymptotic \(L^2(P)\) convergence rates and robustness guarantees modulo additive constants using deep neural networks under possibly asymmetric heavy-tailed noise, attaining the minimax-optimal rate up to logarithmic factors. Numerical experiments demonstrate improvements in estimation accuracy and inferential efficiency over coordinatewise and radial robust methods, alongside stability under orthogonal transformations of the responses. An oral microbiome application further shows that the proposed method identifies more associations that are significant in all examined orthonormal response representations compared with each competing method.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal Risk-Based Hotspot Dynamics Assessment
papers.abstract: Analysis of hotspots often constitutes the final objective in application studies oriented to spatiotemporal risk assessment, particularly for risk mapping and as a helpful instrument for decision making, in diverse fields such as Ecology, Epidemiology, Environmental Sciences, Security, among others. The most primary form, common in practice, consists in identifying and depicting the areas where the magnitude of interest exceeds a certain critical threshold level. In this work, we introduce a wider, more general concept of `hotspot', associated with the extremal values of risk measures defined on different structural indicators of threshold exceedance sets, such as the exceedance area, the excess volume, etc. In particular, we propose a methodological approach based on empirical characterization of the indicator probability distributions from simulation conditional on the available observations, calculated at local resolution scales determined by sliding windows. Risk map generation is then supported by a proper conceptualization and formalization of a suitable family of risk conditional random fields (RCRFs), specified in terms of a set of input elements that can be viewed as flexible tuning parameters for practical implementation and application. For illustration, we consider an extension of a spatiotemporal diffusive blur-generated autoregressive model involving a dynamical spatial deformation. Evolutionary assessment of hotspots is then addressed under different scenarios, with reference to well-known quantile-based risk measures.

papers.title: Realized versus Population Reliability: Anytime-Valid Self-Consistency Certification under Correlated Reasoning
papers.abstract: Self-consistency certification treats repeated sampling from a language model as sequential evidence accumulation and stops when an anytime-valid e-process crosses a threshold, guaranteeing finite-sample Type I error control by Ville's inequality. Prior constructions assume sampled rollouts are conditionally independent. We show this assumption fails in practice: reasoning streams are positively correlated through shared reasoning prefixes or across-prompt heterogeneity, changing not merely certificate efficiency but the hypothesis certified. Modeling dependence via a per-unit latent state (the random-effects / intraclass-correlation structure) induces exchangeable, equi-correlated increments with correlation $\rho$. Correlation splits the single null into a realized null about the drawn belief and a population null about average model behavior, which coincide only when $\rho=0$. We show: (i) the standard betting e-process remains anytime-valid for the realized null, not the population null; (ii) read as a population-null test, a suitable mixture has asymptotic crossing probability at least $\pi=P(\mu(Z)>0)$, potentially exceeding nominal $\epsilon$; (iii) the within-unit mean's effective sample size saturates at $1/\rho$, so extra within-unit rollouts cannot restore population validity; and (iv) a prompt-level e-process restores population validity, with optimal allocation at one rollout per prompt under a pure rollout budget. Simulations and Claude Haiku 4.5 rollouts confirm this regime dependence: on GSM8K ($\hat{\rho}=0.435$, $\hat{\theta}=+0.96$) the gap is dormant, whereas on AIME ($\hat{\rho}=0.480$, $\hat{\theta}=-0.15$) the single-unit rule crosses on 24% of prompts at nominal $\epsilon=0.05$, while the prompt-level procedure declines (0.00). This correctness result identifies which reliability claim an anytime-valid certificate actually supports under dependence.

papers.title: Additive Fréchet Regression for Random Objects
papers.abstract: Regression analysis for complex data taking values in a general metric space has gained increasing attention in recent years, particularly in the context of Fr\'echet regression with Euclidean predictors $\mathbb{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{p}$. However, local Fr\'echet regression, while more flexible than global Fr\'echet regression, suffers from the curse of dimensionality for the case of multivariate predictors. To address this issue while maintaining model flexibility, we introduce a framework of additive structured nonparametric regression when responses are situated in a general metric space. Overcoming the challenge of the lack of vector space structure in general metric spaces where the responses reside requires a novel approach that incorporates the additive structure via projection operators. This leads to a unified framework of additive regression for a wide range of response types, including one-dimensional distributions in Wasserstein space, network data represented by graph Laplacians and spherical data equipped with geodesic distances, among others. We establish pointwise and uniform consistency, including convergence rates, for the proposed additive Fr\'echet regression estimators, using smooth backfitting. The practical utility of this additive model is demonstrated through applications to brain connectivity network analysis using resting-state fMRI data and distributional physical activity data.

papers.title: The Scaled Dirichlet Distribution: Lauricella Representations and Estimation
papers.abstract: We derive explicit expressions for the mixed moments of the scaled Dirichlet distribution in terms of the Lauricella hypergeometric function of type $D$. The relationship with Carlson's multivariate $R$-function is stated, and the convergence conditions required for the series derivation are made explicit. The general expressions yield means, second moments and covariances, with Gauss and Appell hypergeometric representations in the bivariate and trivariate cases. Method-of-moments and maximum-likelihood formulations are presented, together with simulation summaries and an illustrative comparison of scaled Dirichlet and ordinary Dirichlet fits to compositional futures-return data.

papers.title: Networked wealth and mortality in the Agincourt Health and Demographic Surveillance System, 2009--2018
papers.abstract: Background. Though resources embedded in social networks appear to shape health, past studies have not assessed this relationship directly. Using data from Agincourt Health and Demographic Surveillance System in South Africa, we examined the spillover effect of household wealth on mortality in the family network. Methods. We analysed cohort data from 2009 to 2018 to estimate the Average Total Effect (ATE) of household wealth on deaths, decomposing this into an Average Direct Effect (ADE) and Average Spillover Effect (ASE). We estimated these quantities separately for all deaths, deaths among children (<5 years old), premature deaths (among ages 15-59), and deaths among elders (60+). Results. Over the study period, 8750 individuals died. Overall, a one standard deviation increase in household wealth led to an ATE of -0.61% (95% CI: -0.74 to -0.48, P<0.001), an ADE of -0.53% (95% CI: -0.63 to -0.42, P<0.001) and an ASE of -0.08% (95% CI: -0.18 to 0.01, P=0.075). For premature mortality, these effect estimates were -0.37% (95% CI: -0.47 to -0.26, P<0.001), -0.29% (95% CI: -0.37 to -0.21, P<0.001), and -0.08% (95% CI: -0.15 to 0.00, P=0.038), respectively. Conclusions. Results provide evidence for the protective effect of household wealth on premature mortality across family relationships.

papers.title: Fractional Order or False Memory: Identifiability of Caputo SIR Models from Incidence Data
papers.abstract: When a fractional order improves the fit of an epidemic model, it is usually taken as evidence of memory. We ask whether the order of the Caputo susceptible-infectious-removed (SIR) model can actually be recovered from incidence data. If the transmission rate is allowed to vary freely in time, as in hybrid forecasting models, every admissible order, removal rate and initial count reproduces the data exactly. With constant transmission and exact data the order is identifiable in principle, but the dominant term of early linearized growth depends on only two parameter combinations: the growth rate r = (beta - gamma)^(1/alpha) and the amplitude beta*I0/alpha. What is left is transient, and it is limited. We prove that parameter sets sharing these two combinations give Poisson count distributions whose Kullback-Leibler divergence stays bounded no matter how long the linear phase is observed, and that the nonlinear model inherits this bound as the population grows. In simulations, wrong orders were rejected in at most 5% of replicates when the data ended two weeks or more before the epidemic peak, and in 95-100% once the peak was included; separation began only a few days before the peak. With mild overdispersion the order was identified only once about 60% of the population had been infected, and with stronger overdispersion not even then. Fits that the early data could not tell apart predicted peaks that differed by 75%, and plug-in forecasts that ignored parameter uncertainty were badly overconfident. Data generated without any memory produced fitted orders below one when transmission changed and when the fitted model was discretized in daily steps. In early COVID-19 data from Bangladesh and the United States, orders from 0.6 to 1 gave almost the same growth rate, whatever value we assumed for the removal rate.

papers.title: Differentially Private Score Estimation with Applications to Score-Based Generative Models
papers.abstract: Estimating the score function of a distribution plays a central role in statistics and machine learning, with applications in distribution estimation, sampling, and score-based generative modeling. However, learning scores from sensitive data raises privacy concerns. These concerns are particularly pronounced in score-based generative modeling, where trained models may memorize individual training examples and expose sensitive information through membership inference and data extraction attacks. Although non-private score estimation has been extensively studied, the statistical limits of its private counterpart remain less understood. In this work, we study score estimation under $(\alpha,\beta)$-differential privacy for $d$-dimensional sub-Gaussian distributions with locally $\gamma$-H\"older-continuous scores. We develop a sampling-based private score estimator using quadratic B-splines and the exponential mechanism, and we implement our proposal through projected Langevin Monte Carlo with runtime polynomial in the sample size $n$. The proposed estimator satisfies $(\alpha,\beta)$-differential privacy, and achieves expected density-weighted squared error $\mbox{polylog}(n) \max(n^{-2\gamma/(d+2\gamma+2)},\,(n\alpha)^{-2\gamma/(d+\gamma+1)})$. We also establish a nearly matching private minimax lower bound, thereby characterizing the privacy-accuracy trade-off for score estimation. As an application, we construct a differentially private diffusion model whose privacy guarantee is independent of the number of denoising steps. We show that, with an appropriate discretization scheme, the resulting diffusion model attains nearly minimax optimal expected total variation error among all private distribution estimators. We validate our theoretical findings through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

papers.title: Inference in High-Dimensional Linear Mediation Models
papers.abstract: Mediation analysis plays an important role in psychology, epidemiology, and genomics. Al- though high-dimensional mediation has been studied extensively, existing inferential methods typically rely on sparsity assumptions that may be difficult to justify when many individually weak mediators collectively produce a substantial effect. We study inference for both the over- all indirect effect and the effect transmitted through an individual mediator in a proportional high-dimensional regime, where the number of mediators and the sample size grow at compa- rable rates, without imposing sparsity on the mediator effects. Standard debiasing procedures for high-dimensional inference commonly rely on design-covariance information or additional structural assumptions on precision-matrix directions. In mediation models, however, the full outcome-design covariance depends on unknown mediator-model coefficients, creating an addi- tional challenge when such information or structure is unavailable. To address this challenge, we introduce an approximate debiasing procedure based on partial ridge regression and show that the resulting estimator is asymptotically bias-corrected and Gaussian. We also develop a cross-fitted estimator with a smaller asymptotic variance than its sample-split counterpart. In addition, we construct consistent estimators of the limiting variances of both the sample-split and cross-fitted estimators. Together, these results provide feasible inferential procedures for global and pathwise mediation effects.

papers.title: Do Network Mechanisms in Science Vary Across Research Topics? Contextual Relational Hyperevent Models for Large-Scale Bibliometric Data
papers.abstract: Collaboration and citation networks in science are shaped by well-documented mechanisms such as preferential attachment, gender homophily, and self-citation. Whether these mechanisms operate uniformly across research areas, however, is rarely tested, because statistical network models that estimate several mechanisms jointly are difficult to apply to large bibliometric data and to compare across subnetworks. We introduce contextual relational hyperevent models (C-RHEMs), which extend relational hyperevent models by allowing network effects to vary across research topics within a single model. C-RHEMs treat each publication as one event linking its authors to its references, accommodate reference lists spanning several topics, and scale to hundreds of thousands of publications on standard hardware. In a second step, meta-analysis and meta-regression quantify heterogeneity in topic-specific effects and relate it to topic characteristics. We illustrate the approach with about 590,000 oncology publications from the PubMed Knowledge Graph, assigned to 32 OpenAlex research topics. We find that preferential attachment, gender homophily, and self-citation vary substantially across topics, with between-topic standard deviations of 30 to 70 percent of the corresponding pooled effects. Topic age, size, and gender composition account for between a third and two-thirds of this variation: older topics exhibit stronger preferential attachment, self-citation, and gender homophily, and topics with a higher share of male authors exhibit stronger self-citation. The results caution against treating network mechanisms estimated on pooled data as uniform, and C-RHEMs offer a scalable way to study how they differ across research areas.
